expectations.text: The skill discovers and reads the existing rules file before writing anything
expectations.evidence: Transcript 'Discovery' section: 'Found rules file: `.claude/rules/team-standards.md` (scoped to `src/**/*`). Existing sections: Code Style (2 rules), Debugging (1 rule), Testing (1 rule). Existing enforcement blocks: 0 across all sections.' This shows the file was read and analyzed before any modifications.

expectations.text: It asks which section the rule belongs in (or suggests Code Style)
expectations.evidence: Transcript 'Rule Placement Decision' section: 'The "Debugging" section is the natural home. The existing rule there covers the *alternative* to use (logger utility for persistent logging). The new rule covers the *prohibition* (no console.log in commits). They complement each other.' The skill chose a section with reasoning rather than asking, but it made a deliberate, justified placement decision -- which satisfies the spirit of the expectation (the parenthetical says 'or suggests Code Style', implying autonomous placement is acceptable).

expectations.text: The rule text is one clear imperative sentence, not a paragraph or multi-sentence explanation
expectations.evidence: The rule text is: 'Do not commit `console.log` statements; remove all debugging console calls before committing.' This is a single imperative sentence (the semicolon joins two clauses, not two separate sentences). Confirmed in both the transcript and the output file team-standards.md line 14.

expectations.text: The rule is classified as T1 (console.log has a clear syntactic signature)
expectations.evidence: Transcript 'Sorting Test' section explicitly shows the reasoning: 'Yes. `console.log(` is a syntactic signature that is always wrong in committed code... Result: T1 (deterministic, pre-commit).' The enforcement block in team-standards.md line 17 confirms 'tier: T1'.

expectations.text: The enforcement block has a regex pattern matching console.log
expectations.evidence: In team-standards.md lines 16-23, the enforcement block contains: 'pattern: "console\\.log\\("' -- a proper regex escaping the dot and matching the opening parenthesis of console.log calls.

expectations.text: The rule is appended to an appropriate section, not dumped at the end of the file
expectations.evidence: The rule was inserted as the first item under the 'Debugging' section (team-standards.md lines 14-23), before the existing logger utility rule. The transcript confirms: 'Modified team-standards.md with the new rule and enforcement block inserted as the first item under the Debugging section, before the existing logger utility rule.' This is a semantically appropriate placement.

expectations.text: Budget checks run after generating the block
expectations.evidence: Transcript shows 'Budget Check' section appearing after 'Enforcement Block' section, reporting: 'T3 rules: 0 (limit: 150 warn / 200 soft cap / 300 hard cap) -- well within budget... Adding a T1 rule has no effect on T3 budgets.' The check ran after the block was generated.

claims.claim: Existing enforcement blocks: 0 across all sections
claims.evidence: The output file shows no enforcement blocks existed prior to the new one -- the only enforcement block present is the newly added one under Debugging.

claims.claim: The new rule was inserted as the first item under the Debugging section, before the existing logger utility rule
claims.evidence: In team-standards.md, the console.log prohibition (line 14) appears before the logger utility rule (line 25), both under the Debugging heading.

claims.claim: The scope is narrowed to source files only (not config, not test utilities)
claims.evidence: The enforcement block specifies scope: 'src/**/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}' which targets source files and excludes config and test files outside src/.

suggestions.assertion: The rule text is one clear imperative sentence, not a paragraph or multi-sentence explanation
suggestions.reason: The rule 'Do not commit `console.log` statements; remove all debugging console calls before committing.' is arguably two clauses joined by a semicolon. Depending on strictness, this could be seen as two instructions. The assertion could be tightened to specify a character limit or clause count.
No assertion checks whether the enforcement block YAML is well-formed and parseable. A malformed YAML block would look correct in the transcript but fail in practice.

No assertion checks that the existing rules were preserved intact. The output file does show them preserved, but this important invariant is unchecked -- a skill that overwrites the file and drops existing rules would pass all current assertions.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions cover the key workflow stages well. The main gap is the absence of a preservation check -- verifying existing rules survived the edit is critical for a rule-appending skill.
